```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
show <- function(x, cols, digits = 2) {
  knitr::kable(x[, intersect(cols, names(x)), drop = FALSE], digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

## Overview

`lifewatt` reports environmental justice indicators at the granularity each
source actually publishes:

- **by state**: residential electricity price (EIA-861 annual and EIA-861M
  monthly), its trends, a forecast with an interval, and what your own bill
  says about it;
- **by state**: a synthetic life-expectancy estimate built from state death
  rates and the national life table, plus an optional declared
  life-expectancy loss;
- **by ZIP code** (matched to its ZCTA): CDC PLACES adult health prevalence.

No source publishes a realised average residential price per ZIP code, so the
price and life-expectancy functions take a state (a two-letter code or a full
name) and refuse a ZIP by name. Every number in this vignette is computed from
data shipped with the package, except `health_measure()`, which downloads from
data.cdc.gov.

```{r}
library(lifewatt)
```

## 1. What does electricity cost in a state?

The annual price is the customer-weighted mean of the state's utilities.
`price_min` and `price_max` show the cheapest and dearest utility with at least
100 residential customers, so you can see how far a household's own utility
might sit from the state value.

```{r}
annual <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("FL", "TX", "CA", "HI"), electricity_price, year = 2024))
show(annual, c("state", "year", "price", "price_min", "price_max", "n_utility"))
```

The monthly series (2023-01 to 2026-07) flags months that EIA still marks
Preliminary.

```{r}
monthly <- electricity_price("FL", period = "mom")
show(tail(monthly, 4), c("state", "period", "price", "provisional"))
```

The annual and monthly prices are built differently: the annual one averages
utility prices, while the monthly one divides state revenue by state sales. In
most states they agree within a few percent, but not everywhere. Compare like
with like.

```{r}
c(annual_2024 = electricity_price("TX", year = 2024)$price,
  monthly_avg_2024 = mean(price_features("TX", from = "2024-01", to = "2024-12")$price))
```

## 2. Is it going up?

Year-over-year change of the annual price. `monthly_avg_pct_of_prior` gives the
same change computed from the monthly series, and `note` says so when the two
disagree on direction.

```{r}
show(electricity_price_trend("MA", period = "yoy"),
     c("state", "year", "pct_of_prior", "monthly_avg_pct_of_prior"))
```

Month-over-month change:

```{r}
show(tail(electricity_price_trend("FL", period = "mom"), 3),
     c("period", "prior_period", "change", "pct_of_prior", "provisional"))
```

## 3. Is this month expensive?

`price_features()` puts a month in context, in plain units: trailing averages,
changes against last month and last year, the recent trend, and the month
against its trailing 12-month average.

```{r}
pf <- price_features("FL", from = "2026-02", to = "2026-07")
show(pf, c("period", "price", "avg_12m", "change_12m_pct", "trend_12m", "price_vs_avg12m_pct"))
```

`lag_matrix()` puts previous months side by side, for plotting or for your own
model:

```{r}
show(lag_matrix(c("FL", "GA"), from = "2026-06", lags = c(0, 1, 12)),
     c("state", "period", "price_now", "price_1m_ago", "price_12m_ago"))
```

## 4. What will it cost, and what does my bill say?

Months after 2026-07 come from an LSTM forecast. Each forecast row carries a
nominal 85% interval (`price_lo`, `price_hi`). In calibration the forecast ran
low, by 1.7% at one month ahead to 5.2% at five months ahead, and it is not
bias-corrected. A forecast below the last observed month is therefore not, by
itself, evidence that prices will fall.

```{r}
fc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sprintf("2026-%02d", 7:12), function(m) my_electricity("FL", time = m)))
show(fc, c("period", "regime", "price", "price_lo", "price_hi", "price_interval_level"))
```

A bill is treated as evidence. A bill on its own gives the usage it implies;
add the usage and the package turns them into a local price measurement and
blends it with the forecast (inverse-variance weighting).

```{r}
bill_only <- my_electricity("FL", bill = 180, time = "2026-12")
bill_usage <- my_electricity("FL", bill = 180, usage = 1200, time = "2026-12")
show(rbind(bill_only, bill_usage),
     c("evidence_regime", "price", "price_meas", "price_posterior", "price_posterior_sd", "implied_usage_kwh"))
```

When your own price is far from the state price, the row's `notes` say so,
because your utility may well differ from the state average:

```{r}
my_electricity("HI", bill = 180, usage = 1200, time = "2026-12")$notes
```

## 5. Life expectancy

`life_expectancy()` returns a **synthetic** estimate, not an NCHS-published
state life expectancy. It takes the state's age-adjusted death rate relative to
the US, applies it to the national age pattern, and anchors the result to the
national life table. Every assumption is spelled out in
`sensitivity_assumption`.

```{r}
le <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("HI", "FL", "MS"), life_expectancy))
show(le, c("state", "quarter", "e0_synth", "e0_anchor", "rate_state_per_100k", "prop_died_before_75"))
```

For change over time, `e0_change_years` reflects the state's own death rates.
`e0_synth_diff_years` is the plain difference of the two reported values, which
also picks up changes in the national anchor (78.4 for 2023, 79.0 for 2024).

```{r}
tr <- life_expectancy_trend("MS", period = "qoq", quarter = "2024Q1")
show(tr, c("state", "from_quarter", "to_quarter", "rate_change_per_100k",
           "e0_change_years", "e0_synth_diff_years"), digits = 3)
```

The death-rate source is quarterly, so the trend periods are `"yoy"` and
`"qoq"`.

## 6. Expected life-expectancy loss

No sourced US price-to-life-expectancy elasticity exists yet. Without
`delta_le` the loss columns are therefore left empty. With it, you declare a
loss yourself (positive = loss, in years) and the package reports it next to
the price and the national anchor. The closest literature puts an energy-cost
shock at a loss of 0.7 to 2.7 years.

```{r}
ell <- expected_life_loss("FL", "2026-12", bill = 180, usage = 1200, delta_le = 1)
show(ell, c("state", "period", "price", "price_posterior", "e0_anchor",
            "le_loss_years", "le_loss_pct_of_anchor"))
```

## 7. Adult health by ZIP code

`health_measure()` is the one function that takes a ZIP code. It downloads the
CDC PLACES 2025 release (BRFSS 2023 measures) for the matching ZCTA, so it
needs an internet connection and is not run here.

```{r eval = FALSE}
health_measure("32601", measure = c("DIABETES", "BPHIGH"))
```

## Provenance and honesty

Every returned row carries provenance columns (`source`, `level`,
`degraded_from`, `mapping_vintage`, `provisional`) and a `confidence_tier`. On
price and life-expectancy rows `level` is `"state"`. `health_measure()` rows
are `level = "zcta"` with `degraded_from = "zip"`, because a ZIP is treated as
the ZCTA with the same five digits.

How far the state value can sit from a household's own utility is stated on
each price row: `price_min` / `price_max` on the annual row, and
`within_state_sd` (the customer-weighted spread of utility prices) on monthly
and forecast rows.

Inputs that cannot be answered are refused by name, with a pointer to what will
work:

```{r}
tryCatch(electricity_price("32601", year = 2024), error = conditionMessage)
tryCatch(expected_life_loss("FL", "2027-03"), error = conditionMessage)
```
